Even if you can actually make N-gons while 3D modeling, down to the core they're all rendered as triangles, since it's the easiest and fastest to compute. There's no other way to math 3D objects than this, except going mollecular, doing something like voxels but on an incredibly small scale, which would require computers millions of times faster than what the normal consumer can afford.

There's no other way to math 3D objects than this, except going mollecular, doing something like voxels but on an incredibly small scale, which would require computers millions of times faster than what the normal consumer can afford.

That's not strictly true. Current hardware uses triangles because, as you said, it's easy (and subsequently fast). That does not mean it's the only way. You can define objects mathematically (using full blown curve equations). This however does get horribly complex when trying to generate lighting and intersections but not nearly as much as trying to do "molecular voxels".

Most high end ray tracing software does support simple curve primitives that render directly without having to resort to tessellation (converting to multiple tiny polygons). Cylinders, spheres, cones, etc are examples of simple curves. Back in my university days I wrote a (very) simple ray tracer that handled cylinders and spheres exactly (this is in many ways easier than tessellation). Problem is most things are not simple curves. You can start combining simple curves to build more complex things but at some point you end up wasting more resources than an equivalent high resolution tessellation.
